topic: Indus Waters Treaty and India's rejection of the Hague ruling

subtopics.title: Treaty basics and river allocation
subtopics.summary: The Indus Waters Treaty, 1960, is a bilateral water-sharing agreement between India and Pakistan that was facilitated by the World Bank. It allocates the Eastern rivers to India and the Western rivers primarily to Pakistan. India keeps limited, conditional rights on the Western rivers, including run-of-river power generation.
facts: Signed on 19 September 1960, after eight years of negotiations
Bilateral water-sharing agreement between India and Pakistan
Facilitated by the World Bank
Eastern rivers: Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, with exclusive and unrestricted use for India
Western rivers: Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, allocated primarily to Pakistan
India's rights on Western rivers are limited and subject to treaty conditions
Permitted uses on Western rivers include domestic use, limited agricultural use and run-of-river hydroelectric generation
India can build run-of-river hydro projects with minimum storage for conservation and flood management

subtopics.title: Three-tier dispute-resolution mechanism
subtopics.summary: The treaty provides a three-tiered route for disputes, starting with the Permanent Indus Commission for bilateral discussion. Technical differences that the Commission cannot resolve may go to a Neutral Expert, while formal legal disputes may be referred to a Court of Arbitration. The Court of Arbitration is constituted under Annexure G of the treaty.
facts: The treaty provides a three-tiered dispute mechanism
Permanent Indus Commission is the first institutional mechanism and provides a forum for bilateral discussion and information exchange
The Permanent Indus Commission meets at least once a year
Neutral Expert handles technical differences the Commission cannot resolve
The Neutral Expert is appointed through a mechanism involving the World Bank
The Neutral Expert route primarily addresses technical questions
Court of Arbitration handles formal legal disputes referred under the treaty
The Court of Arbitration is constituted under Annexure G and consists of 5 members

subtopics.title: Court of Arbitration's findings
subtopics.summary: The Court of Arbitration held that the treaty continues to apply and that India's decision to place it in abeyance was not permissible. It said the treaty does not deal with terrorism or use of force, so cross-border terrorism was not accepted as a material breach. The tribunal also imposed interim limits on construction at the Ratle project.
facts: The treaty continues in force until terminated by a duly ratified treaty (Article XII(4))
Article III(1) obliges India to let flow the waters of the Western rivers to Pakistan
Placing the treaty in abeyance was held not permissible under the treaty or international law
The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 was applied in the ruling
The treaty does not provide India a unilateral mechanism to suspend obligations
The treaty contains no provisions on terrorism or use of force
Interim limits bar concreting of specified parts of the Ratle dam wall and power intake beyond prescribed levels
The Ratle restrictions last until 90 days after the Neutral Expert's final determination

subtopics.title: India's objection to the tribunal
subtopics.summary: India rejects the ruling, saying the tribunal was constituted by the World Bank contrary to the treaty and has no jurisdiction over its sovereign decisions. India argues the treaty sets a graded, sequential route that ends with a court only after the Neutral Expert step. Pakistan and India initiated parallel proceedings in 2016, and the World Bank paused and later resumed the two processes.
facts: India has rejected the ruling and has neither recognised the tribunal's legitimacy nor participated in its proceedings
India's Ministry of External Affairs says the Court of Arbitration was constituted by the World Bank contrary to the treaty
India's abeyance decision after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack remains valid according to New Delhi
India says the tribunal has no jurisdiction over its sovereign decisions or infrastructure projects on the western rivers
India's position: question, then Permanent Indus Commission, then Neutral Expert, then legal dispute or Court of Arbitration
In 2016, Pakistan initiated proceedings seeking a Court of Arbitration
In 2016, India requested appointment of a Neutral Expert to examine technical aspects
In 2016, the World Bank paused both the arbitration and Neutral Expert processes
In 2022, the World Bank allowed both processes to move forward
India took part in Neutral Expert proceedings but not in Court of Arbitration proceedings

subtopics.title: Indus river system and water-sharing principles
subtopics.summary: The Indus is a trans-boundary river and the longest river in Pakistan, and its main tributaries have distinct sources in Tibet, Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh. The booklet lists three international instruments on shared water: the Helsinki Rules of 1966, the Helsinki Convention of 1992 and the UN Watercourses Convention of 1997. India, China and Pakistan have not signed the UN Watercourses Convention.
facts: The Indus is a trans-boundary river and the longest river in Pakistan
The Indus originates at the Bokhar Chu Glacier near Mt Kailash, Mansarovar, Tibet
The Jhelum rises at the Verinag Spring in the Kashmir Valley and joins the Chenab at Trimmu
The Chenab originates near Bara Lacha Pass in Lahul-Spiti (HP) and joins the Satluj at Panchnad
The Ravi rises in the Kullu Hills near Rohtang Pass and joins the Chenab a little above Rangpur
The Beas originates near Rohtang Pass and joins the Satluj at Harike
The Satluj rises from the Manasarovar-Rakas Lakes in Tibet and joins the Indus a little above Mithankot
Helsinki Rules 1966 were adopted by the International Law Association to regulate water use in an international drainage basin
Helsinki Convention 1992 provides a framework for preventing and controlling water pollution across national borders
UN Watercourses Convention 1997 codified law on non-navigational uses of international watercourses; India, China and Pakistan have not signed it

quizzes.passage:
The Court of Arbitration, which sits in The Hague, examined a dispute over the Indus Waters Treaty. The dispute followed India's decision to place the treaty in abeyance after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack. The case raised a basic legal question: can one party step away from a treaty because of a security crisis, or must the treaty's own terms and the wider law of treaties decide the matter?

The ruling turned on the text of the treaty. The tribunal looked at the provisions on the Western Rivers, the rivers whose waters are central to the case. It also examined whether the treaty has any rules on terrorism or the use of force, since those issues sat in the background of the dispute.

The ruling also concerned a hydroelectric project on the Chenab. The tribunal placed interim limits on certain work at one of these projects, the Ratle project. Those limits are tied to a later stage of the dispute, which involves a technical expert appointed under the treaty.

India has not accepted the ruling. Its government says the tribunal was constituted improperly and has no authority over its sovereign decisions or its projects on the western rivers. The disagreement therefore covers both the substance of the treaty and the legitimacy of the forum that decided it.

quizzes.passage:
A ruling from an international Court of Arbitration has placed the Indus Waters Treaty at the centre of a fresh dispute between India and Pakistan. The treaty has governed the sharing of the Indus river system since 1960, and the question now is whether India could suspend it after a security crisis in 2025. The case asks whether a treaty can be set aside on that basis, or whether it keeps applying until the parties end it through a formal agreement.

The tribunal read the treaty as written and tested India's position against the wider law of treaties. It also considered whether the treaty's text deals with the use of force. These points matter because the answer shapes how the treaty's obligations on the Western Rivers are understood. The ruling is therefore a test of how the treaty's text applies to a new situation.

The ruling also touched on the Ratle project, a hydroelectric scheme in Jammu and Kashmir. Interim limits were placed on some work there, and those limits remain linked to a later stage of the dispute.

India has rejected the ruling and does not accept the tribunal's authority over its decisions on the western rivers. Its objections focus on the tribunal's standing and on the path the dispute took before the tribunal was asked to decide it.

quizzes.passage:
The Indus Waters Treaty is an agreement between India and Pakistan on the river system of the Indus basin. Its rules cover how the waters are shared, and it also sets out how disagreements are to be handled. That second part has become the focus of a recent dispute, because India has rejected a ruling from an international tribunal and has questioned whether the tribunal should have been formed at all.

The debate turns on the structure of the treaty. The two countries read its disputes process differently, and the answer affects which forum can hear a particular question. Each reading leads to a different view of whether the tribunal had any role to play. Both sides refer to the same treaty text, and they differ in how they read it. This difference in reading is at the heart of the dispute.

Parallel moves also matter. In the years before the ruling, both sides pursued processes at the same time, and the institutions involved had to decide how those processes could coexist. That history has given the dispute a procedural side, separate from the questions about water.

India's objections therefore concern procedure, legitimacy and the reach of the tribunal, rather than the flow of the rivers themselves.

quizzes.passage:
A recent ruling has pushed the Indus Waters Treaty back into the news, and with it the question of how disagreements under the treaty should be settled. The treaty contains its own dispute-resolution structure, and the current controversy is about whether that structure was followed. One side has rejected the outcome and has challenged the authority of the tribunal that issued it.

The dispute has a history. Parallel processes were opened in the same period, and the institutions that oversee the treaty had to decide how those processes could run side by side. At one point both were paused, and later both were allowed to move forward again.

The tribunal's findings and the response to them have renewed interest in the treaty's design. The question is not only about how water is allocated but also about process, including which step must come before another and which forum has the final word.

India's government has defended its decision on the treaty and says the tribunal has no power to review it. The dispute therefore turns as much on the order of steps as on the water itself. Several steps in the process are described as separate stages, each with its own role.

quizzes.passage:
The Indus river system is one of the great river systems of South Asia, and its waters are shared by more than one country. The system is made up of a main river and several large tributaries, and each of these rises in a different part of the mountains. Some tributaries begin in high passes and glaciers, while others rise from springs in valleys below.

Because the rivers cross political borders, the way their waters are used is a matter of law as well as geography. Over time, countries and international bodies have developed rules on how shared waters should be managed. These rules cover the use of water in a shared basin and the wider conduct of states that share a watercourse.

The Indus Waters Treaty divides the rivers into two groups, and each group carries different rights for India. The eastern rivers are open to Indian use, while the western rivers are allocated primarily to Pakistan. India keeps some rights over the western rivers, subject to the treaty's conditions.

The booklet describes each river by its sources and by the points where it joins another river. The main tributaries named in the booklet are the Jhelum, the Chenab, the Ravi, the Beas and the Satluj, and each has its own course.

quizzes.passage:
A trans-boundary river system needs rules that every country sharing it can accept. The Indus is one of the most significant examples in South Asia, and its basin is shared by several countries. Its main river rises far to the north, and several large tributaries join it from different directions across the region.

The tributaries have their sources in different places. Some begin in high mountain passes and frozen ice fields, while others come from springs or lakes in the mountains. As they flow, they meet one another at points along the plains, and some of these meeting points lie in Punjab.

Legal thinking about shared rivers developed over several decades. Early work set out principles for the use of water in a shared drainage basin. Later agreements dealt with other concerns, as well as with the wider law governing the non-navigational use of international watercourses.

Not every country has joined the most widely discussed of these agreements. The status of signatures shows which states have accepted the broader framework and which have stayed outside it. The main rivers of the system, including the Jhelum, the Chenab, the Ravi, the Beas and the Satluj, each have their own sources and meeting points.
